extracted.intended_audience: Catholic catechism students / general faithful (children and beginners)
extracted.subtask_description: A question-and-answer catechetical presentation explaining the nature and effects of sin (venial and capital), how to overcome it, and foundational doctrines about the Incarnation, Redemption, and the person of Christ. Aimed at teaching moral and doctrinal standards and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of venial sin
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of venial sin are the lessening of the love of God in our heart, the making us less worthy of His help, and the weakening of the power to resist mortal sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: 'lessening of the love' because it lessens grace; venial sin displeases God though not as greatly as mortal sin. Analogy: a wounded man is easier to kill — a soul weakened by venial sin more easily falls into mortal sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief sources of sin (seven capital sins)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief sources of sin are seven: Pride, Covetousness, Lust, Anger, Gluttony, Envy, and Sloth; commonly called capital sins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a source/spring giving rise to a river — one capital sin (the ruling passion) gathers and produces many other sins. Few have all seven; identify your predominant sin and labor to overcome it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride is an inordinate self-esteem. It comes under the First Commandment because thinking too much of ourselves neglects God and gives to ourselves the honor due to Him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why wrong: worldly goods, appearance, wealth, learning, etc., are transient or from God; excessive care of the body neglects the soul. Followers/examples: conceit, hypocrisy, foolish display in dress or conduct, harshness to others, waste of time on ourselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covetousness / Avarice (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covetousness is an inordinate desire for worldly goods. It comes under the Tenth Commandment and is forbidden by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not sinful: prudent provision for the future. Followers/examples: want of charity, dishonest dealing, theft. Guidance: be content with what one has or can honestly obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lust / Impurity (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lust is the desire for sins of the flesh; for impure thoughts, words, or actions. It comes under the Sixth and Ninth Commandments and is the habit of desiring or violating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Followers/examples: neglect of prayer, neglect of the Sacraments, and possible final loss of faith. Lust and impurity are treated as equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger comes under the Fifth Commandment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Followers/examples: hatred, desire of revenge, and related wrongful acts stemming from uncontrolled anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluttony (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gluttony is the sin of eating or drinking too much: committed by eating too often, being too particular, seeking always costly foods, or by excessive drinking (intemperance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drunkenness: treated as a form of gluttony; leads to loss of reason, violation of God's law, many subsequent sins, injury to health (a kind of slow suicide), neglect of duties, scandal, poverty, and potential insanity. The drunkard is given as an example of cascading evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Envy (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Envy is the desire to see another meet with misfortune so that we may be benefited by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comes under the Eighth Commandment; examples include being glad at another's failure or sorry when they are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sloth (capital sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sloth is committed when we idle our time, are lazy, indifferent about serving God, or do things slowly and poorly as if unwilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences/examples: lying in bed late, neglecting duty, untidiness, misery and want unless supported by others. Sloth relates specially to failing in service to God (First Commandment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominant (ruling) sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person commonly has one capital sin that is the source or root of many other sins — the predominant or ruling passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find and labor to overcome this chief sin; analogy: cutting off the root of an oak rather than repeatedly cutting branches. If the root remains, other sins will regrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three great sins to guard against
rubrics_metrics.description: Three great sins to be always on guard against during life are drunkenness, dishonesty, and impurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: these have most followers and grow gradually without notice; avoiding them greatly reduces likelihood of other sins. Practical guidance: stop inclinations early in youth before they grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to combat sin: root approach and persevering devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Destroy sin by rooting out the capital sin; do not be discouraged if apparent improvement is slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: rowing against a strong tide may not advance but prevents being carried out to sea. Prayer, Mass, and the Sacraments are effective even if immediate progress seems absent — they prevent worsening until temptation weakens and progress can be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incarnation (definition and significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incarnation means to take flesh; here the Son of God taking a true human body — Our Lord's becoming man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: He became man to reveal God and accomplish Redemption; explanation links to later questions on Christ's nature and mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redemption (definition and analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Redemption means to buy back. Christ redeemed mankind by paying the price of His life and blood to free humanity from slavery to sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: slaves cannot redeem themselves; a free man must pay for another's liberty. The Sacrament of Penance is presented as a 'bank' from which one can draw Our Lord's grace merited for us and deposited in the Church.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is the Redeemer
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Blessed Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ is the Redeemer of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit: belief that Christ's life, death, and sacraments provide salvation for mankind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jesus Christ: true God
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the second Person of the Blessed Trinity, true God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He is true and equal to the Father from all eternity; theological affirmation required by faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jesus Christ: true man
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus Christ is true man because He is the Son of the Blessed Virgin Mary and has a body and soul like ours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His human nature was perfect — he shared common human experiences (hunger, thirst, fatigue) but not defects or sin; used to teach about human perfection and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two natures in Jesus Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: In Jesus Christ there are two natures: the nature of God and the nature of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He is one Divine Person with both natures united; the human nature is under the power of the divine will. Mystery acknowledged: accept by faith though full understanding is beyond us.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Blessed Virgin Mary as Mother of God
rubrics_metrics.description: The Blessed Virgin Mary is truly the Mother of God because the same Divine Person who is the Son of God is also the Son of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal affirmation used to explain titles and honor due to Mary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvation before Christ's coming
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who lived before the Son of God became man could be saved by believing in the Redeemer to come and by keeping the Commandments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They were saved through the merits of Our Lord (promised beforehand) and waited in Limbo without suffering until Our Lord opened Heaven. Analogy: a promissory note — salvation was held in the promise of Christ to come.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annunciation Day and Christmas (dates and context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annunciation Day (when the Angel Gabriel announced to Mary she would be Mother of God) is March 25. Christ was born on Christmas Day (December 25) in a stable at Bethlehem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical memory tips given (relation to St. Patrick's and St. Joseph's days); narrative context explaining why Mary and Joseph were in Bethlehem (census) and the humility of Christ's birth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's life length and purpose on earth
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ lived on earth about thirty-three years, and led a most holy life in poverty and suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to show the way to Heaven by His teaching and example across all life stages (infant, child, youth, man). Emphasis on humility and obedience as examples for all ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Passion: what Christ suffered
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus Christ suffered a bloody sweat, a cruel scourging, was crowned with thorns, and was crucified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: Passion began after the Last Supper; explanation of agony in Gethsemane (intense suffering and reasons for it) is introduced.
